claim: GtACR2 is a chloride-conducting channelrhodopsin that has been shown to be more sensitive to light and produce stronger hyperpolarizing currents than other inhibitory opsins.
source: GtACR2, a chloride-conducting channelrhodopsin, was expressed in populations of glutamatergic cells (see 'Materials and methods'). GtACR2 has been shown to be more sensitive to light and produce stronger hyperpolarizing currents than other inhibitory opsins (Govorunova et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Govorunova et al., 2015, which provides external evidence for the properties of GtACR2.

claim: This is the first usage of GtACR2 opsin in the monkey brain.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first usage of this opsin in the monkey brain.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge and review of existing literature, representing an inference about the novelty of their work.

claim: Gene expression of GtACR2 was robust and specific to neurons expressing glutamatergic marker α-CamKII.
source: Gene expression was robust and specific to neurons expressing glutamatergic marker α-CamKII (Figure 1B), with 97% of cells positive for α-CamKII also positive for green fluorescent protein (GFP, co-expressed with GtACR2), and no neurons (NeuN+, a pan-neuronal nuclear antigen marker) that were negative for α-CamKII and positive for GFP (corresponding to inhibitory cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data presented in Figure 1B showing quantitative analysis of cell marker expression.

claim: Light activation reduced firing rates by 24.9% ± 2.1% compared to control trials at the direct suppression site.
source: As expected, light activation reduced firing rates by 24.9% ± 2.1% compared to control trials (mean ± sem, over the entire 300 ms light stimulation interval; 18.1 ± 2.1 sp/s control trials, 11.6 ± 1.4 laser trials, p = 0.0064, Wilcoxon rank sum test, n = 41).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing firing rates between laser and control conditions.

claim: The direct suppression was long-lasting, with responses returning to baseline 387.9 ms ± 38.7 ms after light offset.
source: The direct suppression was long-lasting, and responses returned to baseline 387.9 ms ± 38.7 ms after light offset (median ± sem), consistent with previously measured kinetics of GtACR2 (Govorunova et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements of response kinetics and is consistent with previously published data on GtACR2.

claim: A total of 214 units were recorded across 21 sessions with statistically significant differences in firing rate during laser trials compared to control trials.
source: We recorded a total of 214 units across 21 sessions (both single- and multi-unit responses were included: 127 units from Monkey 1 and 87 units from Monkey 2), with statistically significant differences in firing rate during laser trials compared to control (no laser) trials at one or more visual contrast conditions (Wilcoxon ranked sum test, p<0.005).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data collection and statistical testing across multiple recording sessions.

claim: Firing rates of neurons did not change in the blank 0% contrast condition between laser and control trials.
source: Although firing rates of neurons did not change in the blank 0%, contrast condition (Figure 1F–I; laser vs control trials), the stimulus-triggered responses were highly heterogeneous.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F-I comparing responses in the 0% contrast condition.

claim: The suppressed cells at the off-target site took significantly longer to exhibit response inactivation (92.9 ± 1.1 ms) compared to cells at the direct site (31.2 ± 1.2 ms).
source: As expected from a network-mediated effect, the suppressed cells at the off-target site took significantly longer to exhibit response inactivation (92.9 ± 1.1 ms, mean ± sem) compared to the cells at the direct site (31.2 ± 1.2 ms; p = 0.0007, Wilcoxon ranked sum test).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of suppression latencies between direct and indirect recording sites.

claim: Four basic response patterns emerged following optogenetic inactivation of the nearby network.
source: Across the population, there was a continuum of responses (Figure 2A and C), but four basic response patterns clearly emerged following optogenetic inactivation of the nearby network (see the example cells in Figure 2A and population responses in Figure 2B; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis and visualization in Figure 2A, 2B, 2C, and supplementary figures showing distinct response patterns.

claim: Type 1 responses (suppression across all contrasts) comprised 42.5% of all light-modulated cells.
source: Using this classification strategy in the distal network, we found that a significant fraction of neurons exhibited suppression across all visual stimulus contrasts (labeled Type 1, 42.5% of all light-modulated cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by classification and quantification of recorded neural responses.

claim: Type 2 responses (facilitation at low contrasts and suppression at high contrasts) comprised 28.5% of cells.
source: However, the majority of light-responsive neurons (57.5%) in the distant network exhibited either mixed effects or facilitation—Type 2: facilitation at low contrasts and suppression at high contrasts (28.5% of cells)
evidence: The claim is supported by classification and quantification of recorded neural responses.

claim: Type 3 responses (suppression at low contrasts and facilitation at high contrasts) comprised 20.1% of cells.
source: Type 3: suppression at low contrasts and facilitation at high contrasts (20.1% of cells)
evidence: The claim is supported by classification and quantification of recorded neural responses.

claim: Type 4 responses (facilitation across all contrasts) comprised 8.9% of cells.
source: and Type 4: facilitation across all contrasts (8.9% of cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by classification and quantification of recorded neural responses.

claim: The distal effects cannot be due to direct optogenetic suppression because the distal recording sites are located well within the area targeted by virus injections.
source: Second, the distal recording sites are located well within the area targeted by the virus injections. Injections were spaced across the cortical surface within a rectangular area spanning 1.0 × 0.7 mm (four horizontally spaced columns, with 1 µl × 5 vertically spaced injections in each column; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design and spatial arrangement of virus injections, providing logical inference about the source of observed effects.

claim: 1 µl of a lentiviral suspension has been shown to transfect cells within 1 mm³.
source: Given that 1 µl of a lentiviral suspension has been shown to transfect cells within 1 mm3 (Han et al., 2009), glutamatergic neurons at the distal site would also be expected to express GtACR2 and should be suppressed if exposed to light.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Han et al., 2009, providing external evidence for viral transfection volume.

claim: GtACR2 is much more sensitive to light than traditional channelrhodopsins.
source: This is particularly true since GtACR2 is much more sensitive to light than traditional channelrhodopsins (Govorunova et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Govorunova et al., 2015, providing external evidence for GtACR2 light sensitivity.

claim: Neural responses at the distal sites had no significant light-induced modulation in the absence of visual stimulation.
source: However, we never observed cells exhibiting the characteristic long-lasting suppression at distal recording sites. Further, neural responses at the distal sites had no significant light-induced modulation in the absence of the visual stimulation (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; the 0-contrast condition).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary figures showing no modulation at 0% contrast.

claim: Blue light (473 nm wavelength) is known to scatter rapidly in brain tissue, with virtually no light penetrating laterally beyond the collimated area.
source: Lastly, blue light (473 nm wavelength) is known to scatter rapidly in brain tissue (Diester et al., 2011), with virtually no light penetrating laterally beyond the collimated area (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Diester et al., 2011 and Li et al., 2019, providing external evidence for light scattering properties.

claim: Type 1 responses dominate in supragranular layers, while all types are evenly distributed in granular and infragranular layers.
source: Specifically, Type 1 responses dominate in SG, while all types are evenly distributed in G and IG (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by laminar analysis data shown in Figure 2E and supplementary figures.

claim: Type 1 (purely suppressed) units were evenly distributed throughout all layers, while Type 2, 3, and 4 responses were primarily found in granular and infragranular layers.
source: Type 1 (purely suppressed) units were evenly distributed throughout all layers, while Type 2, 3, and 4 responses were primarily found in G and IG.
evidence: The claim is supported by laminar distribution analysis of response types.

claim: All four response types were found simultaneously within individual recording sessions.
source: Critically, all four response types were found simultaneously within individual recording sessions, when visual stimulus properties and light delivery parameters were identical (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating co-occurrence of response types within sessions.

claim: All sessions with multiple simultaneously recorded neurons had more than one response type.
source: All sessions with multiple simultaneously recorded neurons had more than one response type (data from individual sessions are shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by session-by-session data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The overall proportions of each response type were consistent within sessions and similar across monkeys.
source: The overall proportions of each response type were consistent within sessions (Figure 3A) and similar across monkeys (Figure 3B; p<0.0001, Kruskal-Wallis test, post-hoc Tukey test; within-type comparisons were not significantly different across monkeys, p>0.05).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis comparing response type distributions within and across subjects.

claim: Type 1 cells were sensitive to a broader range of stimulus contrasts (evident by lower slope and higher c50) compared to Type 2 cells.
source: For example, Type 1 cells were sensitive to a broader range of stimulus contrasts (evident by the lower slope, Figure 3F, and higher c50, Figure 3G) and were more strongly modulated by the local network (Figure 3D–E) compared to Type 2 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of normalization model parameters shown in Figures 3D-G.

claim: Type 1 cells were less sensitive to low-contrast stimuli compared to Type 2 or Type 4 cells.
source: Type 1 cells were also less sensitive to low-contrast stimuli compared to Type 2 or Type 4 cells (evident from the higher c50 value, Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of c50 values shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The Type 2 class displayed the lowest values for network inputs compared to other cell classes.
source: The Type 2 class displayed the lowest values for the network inputs (Figure 3D–E) compared to other cell classes.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of normalization model parameters shown in Figures 3D-E.

claim: Non-saturating cells comprised the majority of Type 3 responses (54.8%) and were least represented in the Type 2 group (12.2%).
source: These cells comprised the majority of Type 3 responses (54.8%) and were least represented in the Type 2 group (12.2%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H, I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of non-saturating cells across response types shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The stimulus responses of Type 1, 3, and 4 classes were statistically similar but varied mostly in their additive and divisive network inputs.
source: Interestingly, the stimulus responses (Figure 3F–G) of Type 1, 3, and 4 classes were statistically similar but varied mostly in their additive and divisive network inputs (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of normalization model parameters across response types.

claim: Modulating local network sensitivity alone (while keeping feedforward input and E/I ratio fixed) can reproduce all four types of responses observed experimentally.
source: Our crucial observation was that modulating local network sensitivity alone (while keeping feedforward input and E/I ratio fixed) can reproduce all four types of responses observed experimentally (Figure 4B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 4B-E.

claim: Altering the sensitivity of the feedforward gain (rather than the local excitatory network gain) did not reproduce all four experimentally observed response motifs.
source: We also tested the effect of altering the sensitivity of the feedforward gain (rather than the local excitatory network gain), but this manipulation did not reproduce all four experimentally observed response motifs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in supplementary figures.

claim: For a limited range of E/I ratios (1.95–2), all four response types can be generated solely by altering the local network sensitivity.
source: We found that for a limited range of E/I ratios (1.95–2), all four response types can be generated solely by altering the local network sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling analysis of parameter space.

claim: There is no equivalent range of network sensitivity values that could produce all four response types if only the E/I ratio is modulated.
source: However, there is no equivalent range of network sensitivity values that could produce all four response types if only the E/I ratio is modulated.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling analysis of parameter space.

claim: Behavioral performance was significantly changed on 57.9% of laser suppression trials compared to control trials (31.6% impaired and 26.3% facilitated).
source: Across daily sessions and contrast conditions, we found that behavioral performance was significantly changed on 57.9% of laser suppression trials compared to control trials (31.6% impaired and 26.3% facilitated; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data analysis shown in supplementary figures.

claim: In Type 1 dominant sessions, detection performance was impaired on laser trials (9.3 ± 1.9%) compared to control trials (19.5 ± 5.1%) for the lowest contrast stimuli.
source: Across the 10 sessions dominated by Type 1 responses, we found that detection performance was impaired on laser trials (target reports on laser trials: 9.3 ± 1.9%; control trials: 19.5 ± 5.1%, mean ± sem) for the lowest contrast stimuli (Figure 5B; p = 0.04, t-test, paired, two-way)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral performance data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In sessions with highly heterogeneous V1 responses, detection performance remained unchanged between laser and control trials for both low and high contrasts.
source: However, in the sessions in which V1 responses were highly heterogeneous, detection performance remained unchanged between laser and control trials both for the low (Figure 5E–F; p = 0.40, t-test, paired, two-way) and high contrasts (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral performance data shown in Figure 5E-F and supplementary figures.

claim: For Type 2 dominant sessions, there was a significant impairment in detection performance at 20% contrast in laser trials compared to control.
source: For a subset of these mixed-type sessions, where Type 2 responses were dominant ( >35% of Type 2 cells recorded, n = 6 sessions; Figure 5—figure supplement 1F, p = 0.0032, one-way Kruskal-Wallis, df = 3, Chi-sq = 13.8, post-hoc t-test), we found a significant impairment in detection performance at the 20% contrast in laser trials compared to control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, G, H; p = 0.016, t-test, paired, two-way)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral performance data in Type 2 dominant sessions shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Across sessions and stimulus conditions, there was no significant difference in eye position between laser and control conditions.
source: However, across sessions and stimulus conditions, we did not observe a significant difference in eye position (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, B, D, E; median p-value = 0.493, Wilcoxon ranked sum test)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of eye tracking data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: There was no significant difference in pupil size between laser and control conditions across sessions and stimulus conditions.
source: or pupil size (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C, F; median p-value = 0.498, Wilcoxon ranked sum test) between laser and control conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of pupil size measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: There were no statistically significant differences in eye movements and pupil size between Type 1 dominant and mixed-type sessions.
source: Importantly, there were no statistically significant differences (p>0.1) in eye movements and pupil size between Type 1 dominant and mixed-type sessions.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical comparison of eye tracking and pupil measurements across session types.

claim: Consistent behavioral changes were only observed when neuronal responses at both the optogenetically targeted site and the off-target distal sites were suppressed.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that consistent behavioral changes were only observed when neuronal responses at the optogenetically targeted site and at the off-target distal sites were both suppressed.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined behavioral and neural data across different session types.

claim: When the distal neural population is dominated by heterogeneous changes in firing rates, changes in behavioral choices are mixed and inconsistent across sessions.
source: When the distal neural population is dominated by heterogeneous changes in firing rates, changes in behavioral choices are mixed and inconsistent across sessions.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the combined behavioral and neural data across different session types.

claim: Focal optogenetic suppression induces complex changes in the functional properties of nearby neural populations.
source: Our study demonstrates that focal optogenetic suppression induces complex changes in the functional properties of nearby neural populations.
evidence: The claim summarizes the overall findings from the experimental data presented throughout the study.

claim: Cortical inactivation did not result in a simple distance-based decay effect of suppression as a function of proximity to light source.
source: Contrary to our expectation, cortical inactivation did not result in a simple distance-based decay effect of suppression as a function of proximity to light source.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed heterogeneous response patterns rather than uniform suppression.

claim: Complex changes in responses during suppression of distal cortical activity were predominantly present in deeper cortical layers.
source: Furthermore, complex changes in responses during suppression of distal cortical activity were predominantly present in deeper cortical layers, and hence studies limiting electrophysiological (Nassi et al., 2015; Sato et al., 2014) and optical recordings (Michel et al., 2018) to superficial layers would underestimate these important network effects.
evidence: The claim is based on the laminar distribution data and is supported by inference about implications for other studies with citations.

claim: The mixed off-target effects could possibly explain the highly variable changes in behavioral performance during optogenetic inactivation observed in non-human primate studies.
source: We suggest that the mixed off-target effects found here could possibly explain the highly variable changes in behavioral performance during optogenetic inactivation, particularly observed in non-human primate studies (Dai et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a possible explanation for variability in other studies with a supporting citation.

claim: The local network is a source of normalizing drive to cortical neurons.
source: Furthermore, our results provide strong experimental support for prior untested hypotheses that the local network is a source of normalizing drive to cortical neurons.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data showing network-mediated effects consistent with normalization.

claim: Normalization has been proposed to be one of the canonical computations in the cortex.
source: Normalization has been proposed to be one of the canonical computations in the cortex (Carandini and Heeger, 2011); yet it presently lacks a clear mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Carandini and Heeger, 2011, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: The normalizing input from the local network is not uniform, but rather is idiosyncratically tailored for each neuron.
source: We have shown here that the local network does indeed provide normalizing inputs to neurons within a column. However, this normalizing input is not uniform, but rather it is idiosyncratically tailored for each neuron.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observed heterogeneity in response types and normalization parameters.

claim: Type 3 and Type 4 response motifs, with their instances of response augmentation at high contrasts, have never been previously described.
source: Type 3 and Type 4 response motifs, in particular, with their rather surprising instances of response augmentation at high contrasts, have never been previously described.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature, representing an inference about the novelty of these findings.

claim: Normalization has been shown to stabilize neural responses and thus reduce variability to repeated stimulus presentations.
source: For example, normalization has been shown to stabilize neural responses and thus reduce variability to repeated stimulus presentations (Coen-Cagli and Solomon, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Coen-Cagli and Solomon, 2019, providing external evidence for the function of normalization.

claim: Parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons in mouse visual cortex are believed to be critically involved in the gain modulation of nearby pyramidal neurons.
source: In mouse visual cortex, parvalbumin-positive (PV) interneurons are believed to be critically involved in the gain modulation of nearby pyramidal neurons (Atallah et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Atallah et al., 2012 and Wilson et al., 2012, providing external evidence from mouse studies.

claim: PV interneurons in mouse auditory cortex do not modulate the overall gain of local pyramidal cells in a stimulus-dependent manner.
source: However, PV interneurons in mouse auditory cortex do not modulate the overall gain of local pyramidal cells in a stimulus-dependent manner, as would be required by contrast normalization mechanisms (Cooke et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cooke et al., 2020, providing external evidence from mouse auditory cortex studies.

claim: Axons of basket cells in cat visual cortex can target neurons up to 1360 μm away and do not obey orientation domain boundaries.
source: For instance, axons of basket cells (morphologically defined PV cells [Scala et al., 2020]) in cat visual cortex can target neurons up to 1360 μm away and do not obey orientation domain boundaries, with 57% of projections synapsing at sites with orientation preferences differing by >30° from the location of the basket cell's soma (Kisvárday et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Scala et al., 2020 and Kisvárday et al., 1994, providing external evidence from cat visual cortex studies.

claim: Previous studies silencing cortical populations have primarily focused on the light-targeted zone without investigating collateral effects on the nearby local network.
source: Previous studies silencing cortical populations, particularly those using optogenetic tools, have primarily focused on the light-targeted zone without investigating collateral effects on the nearby local network (Diester et al., 2011; Fetsch et al., 2018; Han et al., 2011; Nassi et al., 2015; Ohayon et al., 2013; Trouche et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous optogenetic studies, representing a review of existing literature.

claim: Crook and Eysel (1992) showed that inactivating visual cortex using GABA microiontophoresis could substantially broaden tuning curves of neurons located 600 microns away.
source: Crook and Eysel, 1992 have previously shown that inactivating visual cortex, using gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) microiontophoresis, could substantially broaden tuning curves of neurons located 600 microns away, but only if the inactivated site had a preferred orientation drastically different from the recording site.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Crook and Eysel, 1992, providing external evidence from a previous inactivation study.

claim: Li et al. (2019) examined the effects of cortical inactivation on more distant cortical sites by comparing the spatiotemporal profiles of several suppressive opsin constructs in awake mice.
source: A recent study by Li et al., 2019 examined the effects of cortical inactivation on more distant cortical sites by comparing the spatiotemporal profiles of several suppressive opsin constructs in awake, but otherwise passive, mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2019, providing external evidence from a recent mouse study.

claim: Heterogeneous responses emerged only when optogenetic suppression was paired with a visual stimulus.
source: Similarly, we found that in the absence of a visual stimulus (the 0% contrast condition), firing rates in the distal network are not significantly influenced by optogenetic suppression (Figure 1F–I, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Heterogeneous responses emerged only when optogenetic suppression was paired with a visual stimulus.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the data showing no modulation at 0% contrast but heterogeneous responses with visual stimuli.

claim: The presence of stimulus in visual cortex activates otherwise minimal local network connections to produce characteristic response features such as contrast normalization and near-surround suppression.
source: This detail is important because the presence of stimulus in visual cortex activates otherwise minimal local network connections to produce characteristic response features such as contrast normalization and near-surround suppression.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about visual cortex function and inference from the experimental results.

claim: The lentiviral vector LV-CaMKIIα-GtACR2-GFP was prepared by the University of North Carolina Vector Core with a titer of 10^9 IU/ml.
source: The anion channelrhodopsin GtACR2 (Forli et al., 2018; Govorunova et al., 2015; Mauss et al., 2017; Mohammad et al., 2017) was packaged in a lentiviral construct under the control of the promoter α-CamKII (LV-CaMKIIα-GtACR2-GFP). The vector was prepared by the University of North Carolina Vector Core, with a titer of 109 IU/ml.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the experimental materials and methods used.

claim: Four V1 columns, and five sites per column (spaced every 250 µm), were targeted for injection per animal.
source: Four V1 columns, and five sites per column (spaced every 250 µm), were targeted for injection per animal.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the experimental injection protocol.

claim: For each injected column, 1 µl of the viral suspension was delivered over a 10 min period at each site.
source: After a 15min waiting period (5 min waiting period for every subsequent site within the column), the plunger was independently advanced, delivering 1 µl of the viral suspension over a 10 min period.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the experimental injection protocol.

claim: Monkeys completed a contrast detection task using sine-wave gratings presented at the recorded cell population's preferred orientation and a fixed spatial frequency.
source: Monkeys completed a contrast detection task using sine-wave gratings presented at recorded cell population's preferred orientation and a fixed spatial frequency.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the behavioral task design.

claim: On 50% of trials, optical stimulation was delivered simultaneously with the visual stimulus.
source: Additionally, on half of the trials, optical stimulation was delivered simultaneously with the visual stimulus (or when the visual stimulus would have appeared on a no-stimulus trial) and was delivered equally throughout all stimulus contrast conditions.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the experimental design.

claim: Stimuli had a median size of 2.5° (± 0.6°) and a spatial frequency of 2 cycles per degree.
source: Stimuli had a median size of 2.5° (± 0.6°) and a spatial frequency of 2 cycles per degree.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the visual stimulus parameters.

claim: Light power output at the end of the fiber optic was kept consistent across sessions at approximately 7–14 mW per mm².
source: Light power output at the end of the fiber optic was periodically measured using an integrating sphere sensor (S124C, Thor Labs) and was kept consistent across sessions (~7–14 mW per mm2).
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the optogenetic stimulation parameters.

claim: The optical fiber was scissor-cut and the direction of the light was perpendicular to the cortical surface.
source: Importantly, the optical fiber was scissor-cut and the direction of the light was perpendicular to the cortical surface, meaning that the maximum light power was vertical, parallel to cortical columns.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the optogenetic stimulation setup.

claim: On average, per session, 5 (± 4) single units and 7 (± 3.5) units whose activity could be significantly modulated by light application were identified.
source: On average, per session, we were able to identify 5 (± 4) single units and 7 (± 3.5) units (single or multiunit activity) whose activity could be significantly modulated by light application.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the data collection results.

claim: For the majority of units (72.9%), the peak response averaged across stimuli occurred in 150–300 ms after stimulus onset.
source: For the majority of units (72.9%), the peak response averaged across stimuli occurred in 150–300 ms after stimulus onset.
evidence: The claim is a factual statement about the temporal characteristics of neural responses.
